explain.say: A high-speed train cruising at 300 kilometres per hour has forces acting on it in every direction. Its weight pulls down, and the rails push up with an equal force, so it does not move up or down.

explain.say: Steel wheels on steel rails have very low rolling resistance, much less than rubber tyres on a road, which is one reason trains are so efficient. When the driving force equals all the resistance, the forces balance and the train cruises steadily.

faq.a: Electric motors turn the wheels, and friction between the steel wheels and rails pushes the train forward. Without that grip, called adhesion, the wheels would just spin.
asks: What is adhesion on a railway?

faq.q: Why is air resistance so big for fast trains?
faq.a: Air resistance grows with the square of speed: twice as fast means about four times the drag. At 300 kilometres per hour most of the power goes into pushing air aside.
asks: What slows a fast train down?

faq.q: Why do trains have low rolling resistance?
faq.a: Hard steel wheels on hard steel rails barely squash, so very little energy is lost as they roll. A rubber tyre squashes much more and wastes more energy.

faq.q: Why doesn't a train sink into the track or lift off?
faq.a: The rails push up on the wheels with a force equal to the train's weight, so the up and down forces balance.

faq.q: What happens when the forces on a train balance?
faq.a: When the driving force equals air and rolling resistance together, there is no overall force, so the train keeps going at a steady speed. That is Newton's first law.
asks: Why does a train move at a steady speed?

facts: Japan's first Shinkansen high-speed line opened in 1964.
A French TGV set the world speed record for a wheeled train, 574.8 kilometres per hour, in 2007.
Steel wheels on steel rails have much lower rolling resistance than rubber tyres on roads.

quiz.why: At steady speed the driving force equals air and rolling resistance, so there is no overall force.

wrong.1: A bigger driving force would make the train speed up, not cruise steadily.
